title: Admiration May Be the Most Underrated Leadership Tool
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that admiration is the most underutilized emotional tool in a leader's repertoire — not because it is rare, but because leaders are trained to seek admiration rather than give it. The article distinguishes admiration sharply from praise and flattery: while those are things leaders say on cue, admiration is an emotion leaders feel through genuine observation and reflection on what is exceptional in another person. Because admiration signals what a leader truly values, it functions as a kind of thermostat for team behavior — when leaders admire boldness, people take more risks; when they admire precision, people slow down and get it right. The article's key psychological claim is that admiration shapes self-identity: people strive to become the version of themselves that their leaders admire, making the leader's admiration a mirror into which people grow. The best leaders hold a high bar for what counts as admirable but say so specifically and quickly when something clears it. The conclusion is that admiration costs nothing, requires no formal authority, and carries no agenda — yet it builds cultures where people reach higher and invest more fully in their work and in each other.
points: Admiration is categorically different from praise or flattery — it is an emotion leaders feel through observation, not a verbal habit triggered by performance, and this authenticity is what gives it transformative power over self-identity.

The thermostat effect: what a leader publicly admires sets behavioral norms for the entire team — admiring boldness produces risk-takers, admiring precision produces careful workers, making admiration an invisible operating system for culture.

Being genuinely admired by someone you respect is one of the most powerful motivators in human experience — not just emotionally rewarding, but self-defining — because it tells you who your admirer believes you can become.
The best leaders hold a high bar for what counts as admirable — they are not reflexively positive — but when something genuinely clears that bar, they are quick to name it specifically and candidly.
Admiration costs nothing and requires no formal authority; yet its impact is to build cultures where people reach higher, try harder, and invest more fully in their work and in each other.
quotes: Of the 27 emotions identified by psychologists, admiration is perhaps the most underrated and underleveraged by leaders. That's because leaders are taught to seek admiration, not to find and give it.

Admiration signals what a leader values and reveals what they believe matters most. Being genuinely admired by someone you respect is one of the most powerful motivators in human experience. It doesn't just feel good. It shapes self-identity.

Admiration felt and expressed by leaders sets the thermostat for how people operate. When a leader admires boldness, people take more risks. When they admire precision, people slow down and get it right.
People strive to become the version of themselves that their leaders admire. In that sense, admiration creates a mirror, and people grow into the reflection.

Unlike praise or flattery, which are things leaders say, admiration is an emotion leaders feel through observation and reflection. It is always highly specific and arises from what leaders find exceptional and impressive in others.

The best leaders are more likely to admire the effort behind what a person does, the way they do it, and what it says about their character rather than just their outcomes or results. They are acutely aware of what they admire and why.

Admiration costs nothing, does not require formal authority, and carries no agenda. It is simply honest, specific recognition of what a leader genuinely finds exceptional in another person. Yet its impact is transformative.
